title: The Mystery of the Melting Ice
markdown:
Hugo the hippo let out a sigh that puffed warm mist into the frosty air. He stood beside Pearl the penguin, admiring their handiwork, or trying to. For the annual Winter Fair they were in charge of the school’s ice display. Usually this was their favourite job. They loved the tingle of cold and the satisfying thwack of mallets on frozen water.

“It’s looking a little peculiar this year, Hugo,” Pearl chirped, tilting her head. Her tuxedo was neat as ever. Her beady eyes held puzzlement.

Hugo adjusted the small round spectacles that perched unsteadily on his wide snout. “Peculiar is one way to put it. I was thinking more… wiggly.”

The trouble was not the ice at first. It was supposed to be solid gleaming blocks, just right for fancy shapes. As soon as they set a new block down, an odd thing happened. It melted, but not just anywhere. It melted into a clear arrow, pointing away from their planned display. Thwip. Thwip. Thwip, went the slow drips.

“It’s almost as if the ice is trying to show us something,” Pearl mused, tapping a flipper on her chin. “Or escape.”

Hugo’s tummy did an unpleasant flip. He reached into his pocket for the smooth grey river stone he always carried, a reminder of calm water. He liked things neat, orderly, predictable. Arrowing ice was none of those. The fair was two days away. A muddled mess because he had not been organised enough: that thought sat down in him and made itself at home.

“We must get to the bottom of this, Pearl,” he said, trying to sound braver than his spectacles. He gave them a nudge. “Before the fair, the display must be perfect. No messy arrowy ice.”

Pearl’s small wings flapped purpose. “Let’s follow the arrows. They must be leading somewhere.”

They put on scarves. Pearl brought a notebook of her own, mostly doodles of fish. Hugo brought extra spectacles in case the first pair steamed. The first arrow, surprisingly sharp, pointed to the old forgotten shed at the edge of the grounds. They circled it once. Nothing but a rusted watering can and a smell of last autumn. The second arrow led past it, through a tangle of bushes that tickled Hugo’s knees and left burrs on Pearl’s neat tuxedo. She picked them off without complaining, which Hugo found heroic in a small way. The third, the most insistent, pointed at the base of a large ivy-covered wall. A drip from the last block they had carried still marked the snow behind them, as if the ice were insisting they not lose the thread.

“A most unusual path,” Hugo whispered, breath in little clouds. He peered at the ivy, a velvety curtain. The wall looked wobbly, and he did not like wobbly things. Heights and unsteadiness made him queasy. He turned the stone in his pocket until it was warm.

Pearl was already investigating. “Look. A little handle.” She tugged. With a long groan a section of wall swung inward, a dark opening, dust and old-thing smell, cool damp air, a forgotten quiet.

They stepped in. A narrow winding passage, dimly lit by thin shafts of sun through cracks. Hugo’s large feet thudded. Pearl’s flippers clicked, cheerful even here. The passage twisted like a sleepy snake. Once it forked, and they chose the way that still felt cold, because ice would have wanted that. A shelf of jam jars, labels faded to mystery, watched them pass. Then a rickety ladder leaned against a high opening. A draught came down it that smelled of stone and old winter.

Hugo’s heart did a frantic thump-thump-thump. Palms slick. The dark space above looked like a mouth that had not decided to be kind. He almost turned back. The stone in his pocket felt suddenly not enough.

Pearl nudged his grey leg with her beak. “It’s quite all right. I can go first. I’m small. I can check.”

She scampered up with astonishing speed. “Perfectly fine. Just a little dusty.”

Relief let him climb, stiff and careful, each rung a decision. Deeper they went, until the passage opened into a surprisingly large dusty room. Strange old devices. Shelves of forgotten treasure and forgotten junk. In the centre, gleaming faintly: sturdy old-fashioned ice tools — sharp chisels, strong saws, a beautiful smooth mallet. Beside them a thick leather-bound notebook, waiting as if it had been practising patience.

Pearl nudged it open. “This looks awfully important.” Her beak moved down the pages. Diagrams. Dates. A hand that had loved order as much as Hugo did. “How to keep ice perfectly solid. A special technique. Less water. More chill. Night pouring. Morning carving.” She giggled. “A secret recipe for super-strong ice.”

Hugo’s anxiety began to melt at the edges. He turned a chisel in his big careful hands. The tools looked more robust than theirs, the sort made by someone who expected winter to argue back. “This is exactly what we needed.” He thought of the two days left and found, for the first time that week, that two days sounded like enough.

Pearl pointed to a particularly strong chisel half-hidden under canvas. “To get this, and the notebook, we have to move that big lever. It is stuck. It will need a good push.” She puffed her chest. “I think I can do it.” Her voice wavered a tiny bit. Hugo saw she would spend every last bit of herself on it.

He looked at his pocket. The river stone. A trip with his mum. An anchor. Leaving it felt like leaving a small piece of the calm self he preferred. He looked at Pearl’s determined face.

He traced the stone once more, then set it on a dusty shelf.

Pearl braced. Creak. Groan. Squeeeeak. The lever moved. The chisel and notebook slid free. Pearl slumped, panting, spent in the useful way.

They gathered the treasures and climbed back. The dark corners felt less like a scolding and more like a place that had been waiting for two people who would put things back to use. Outside, the sun was dipping, orange and pink on the snow.

At the display they worked with the notebook’s clear instructions and the old tools. Less water. More chill. Pearl read a line, Hugo cut, Pearl checked the edge with a flipper as if tasting weather. The ice held. It took a shape and kept it: a swan that did not droop, a castle with windows that stayed windows. Hugo hummed. He did not reach for his pocket. He felt steady, which was a surprise he decided to keep. When a drip started on one corner he did not panic. He turned the block the way the notebook said, and the drip thought better of being an arrow.

The Winter Fair was a grand success. Bunting snapped in a polite wind. Someone sold hot blackcurrant that stained mouths a cheerful purple. The display stood tall and gleaming, no melting arrows, in the middle of the yard where last year a puddle had made a map of failure. Children gasped at the sculptures. A small hippo asked Hugo how the swan’s neck stayed up. Hugo, who would once have reached for his stone, showed the notebook page instead, and the small hippo nodded as if chill were a spell you could learn. Teachers beamed and said Hugo and Pearl’s names as if the names themselves were a kind of ice that did not drip.

As they packed the last tools, Pearl spotted something small and grey on the dusty shelf. Hugo looked at the stone, then at her. He could collect it later. Pearl was already helping a much younger penguin carry a sparkling icicle, doing little happy hops, not tired at all.

Hugo breathed the cool air. The creak of the lever, when he remembered it, sounded less like a struggle and more like a tool agreeing to work. He left the stone where it was until the packing was done, which was a small new habit, and a good one.
characters: Hugo (a hippo who likes things orderly), Pearl (a penguin)
